content.p: Bryan Kohberger was a criminal justice doctoral student when, in the early hours of 13 November 2022, four University of Idaho students were stabbed to death in an off-campus house on King Road in Moscow, Idaho. On 2 July 2025 he pleaded guilty in Boise to the four murders and a burglary charge, in a deal that took the death penalty off the table. On 23 July 2025 Judge Steven Hippler sentenced him to four consecutive terms of life in prison without parole, plus 10 years for the burglary.

The case ended without a trial and without an explanation. Kohberger answered "yes" when the judge asked whether he had killed each of the four victims, but he never said why, and he declined to speak at his sentencing. In July 2026 he reversed his position with a court filing in which he appears to represent himself: a petition asking to withdraw the plea, along with a claim that he is innocent.

Kaylee Goncalves and Madison Mogen, both 21, and Xana Kernodle, 20, shared the house on King Road. Kernodle was dating Ethan Chapin, 20, who had stayed the night. Two other students who lived there, Bethany Funke and Dylan Mortensen, were also at home but were not attacked.

The housemates had spent the day before in ordinary ways, according to Funke's account to Moscow police, which was released after the sentencing. They ate Taco Bell, napped, went to a daytime party and then a second house party. Goncalves and Mogen went on to a bar and a food truck in downtown Moscow before getting a ride home, according to a police affidavit cited by NPR. Their roommates told police that all four were back by 2 a.m. and had gone to their rooms by 4 a.m., about when Kernodle received a DoorDash delivery order.

Mortensen, who lived on the second floor and is identified in the early court documents only as "D.M.", told police she woke after 4 a.m. to strange noises and crying. Looking out, she saw what appeared to be a man in a mask walking toward her, and he passed her as she stood frozen. He then headed for the rear sliding door. She locked her door and texted and called her roommates. At around noon she asked friends to come to the house, and when one of them went upstairs and found blood in Kernodle's room, he told everyone to leave and called the police. CNN, citing records, said Funke dialled 911 at 11:56 a.m. and reported that Kernodle was unconscious.
content.h2: The trail to a white Hyundai
content.p: Surveillance cameras recorded a car of that type, a white Hyundai Elantra, passing the house several times between about 3 a.m. and 4 a.m., including an attempt to park or turn around in front of it, according to the police affidavit as NPR described it. The car left at what the affidavit called a high rate of speed at about 4:20 a.m. When Moscow police asked nearby agencies to look out for such a car, two Washington State University officers flagged Kohberger's, and a Moscow officer noted that his driver's licence details matched the roommate's description of the masked figure.

Police already had his phone number from an earlier traffic stop. According to the affidavit, the phone dropped off the network from 2:47 a.m. until 4:48 a.m. on the morning of the killings, and when it reconnected it was on a highway south of Moscow, then moving back toward Pullman.

The decisive piece was DNA. A tan leather sheath bearing a Ka-Bar logo had been left on the bed next to Mogen, and laboratory technicians recovered a single source of male DNA from its button snap, the affidavit said. Investigators in Pennsylvania, where Kohberger's family lives, retrieved discarded trash from their home in Albrightsville. DNA from it suggested a close family relationship to the sheath sample. Pennsylvania police then arrested Kohberger, and he was extradited to Idaho. CBS News gave the arrest date as six weeks after the killings, and Rolling Stone gave it as 30 December 2022.

When a grand jury indicted him in May 2023, Kohberger chose to "stand silent" rather than plead, and the judge entered not guilty pleas on his behalf, according to Rolling Stone. His attempts to have the case dismissed were rebuffed in October 2023. In 2024 the trial was moved out of Latah County to Boise because of concern that publicity and statements by local officials would make a fair jury impossible, CBS News reported.

Prosecutors signalled early that they would seek the death penalty. A defence motion to remove it as a possible sentence was denied in November 2024, and in April 2025 a judge rejected the argument that a recent autism diagnosis made a death sentence cruel and unusual. Days before the plea became public, Hippler also refused to let the defence tell jurors that four "alternate perpetrators" could have committed the killings. He called the argument "rank speculation" and wrote that the evidence about those four people was "entirely irrelevant". NPR reported that the four had given DNA and fingerprint samples and were not connected to the scene. Jury selection was due to start in August 2025, with the trial expected to run through November.

The agreement surfaced on the last weekend of June 2025. The Latah County Prosecutor's Office emailed the victims' families on Sunday night with a letter attached. In the letter, the office said Kohberger's lawyers had asked for the deal and that he had accepted it. Hippler said he learned of it on Monday afternoon, while his staff were preparing to bring in as many as 10,000 people to fill out jury questionnaires.

The families were divided. The Goncalves family said they were "beyond furious" and asked for a plea that required a full confession, the location of the weapon and confirmation that he acted alone. Afterwards they said the plea "represented an easy way out and no answers". Mogen's father, Ben Mogen, said he was relieved, and the Mogen family said they supported the agreement "100%". Kernodle's father, Jeff Kernodle, told the New York Times it was hard to accept that there would be no trial.

At the hearing on 2 July 2025, Hippler asked Kohberger whether he was pleading guilty because he was guilty. Kohberger said he agreed with the deal, understood the charges and had not been coerced. He answered "Yes" as the judge named each victim and asked whether he had murdered that person. The agreement called for consecutive fixed life terms, waived his right to appeal and to ask for leniency, and spared him a death sentence. Hippler said the court was not bound by the agreement on sentencing but that Kohberger could not ask for anything different.
content.h2: The evidence the prosecutor laid out
content.p: Because there was no trial, the account Thompson gave at the plea hearing is the fullest public statement of the state's case. He said that Kohberger bought a Ka-Bar knife from Amazon in March 2022, and that the knife was determined to be the weapon. He had moved to Pullman in June 2022 for his doctorate at Washington State. From 9 July 2022 his phone connected 23 times, late at night or in the early morning, to a cell tower serving the area of the King Road house, and Thompson said it was unclear whether he made direct contact with any of the residents on those trips. Moscow police had also recorded his identity and his 2015 white Hyundai Elantra at a traffic stop on 22 August 2022.

On the night itself, Thompson said, Kohberger left his Pullman apartment with his phone turned off, and surveillance footage showed his car circling the King Road area before it parked behind the house shortly after 4 a.m. He said Kohberger came in through the kitchen sliding door at the back, killed Mogen and Goncalves on the third floor, then met Kernodle, who was still awake, on the way down and killed her and Chapin. A sheath was left on the bed beside Mogen. A neighbour's camera caught the car speeding away, Thompson said, so fast that the driver nearly lost control. The phone came back on at about 4:48 a.m. and, according to Thompson, Kohberger took a thumbs-up selfie in his apartment bathroom at 9:30 that morning.

Afterwards, Thompson said, Kohberger searched again for the type of knife on Amazon and tried to delete or alter his purchase history, and he changed his car registration from Pennsylvania to Washington. Police found the car had been "meticulously cleaned" inside, which Thompson linked to a paper Kohberger had written on crime-scene processing. The knife was never recovered. Thompson also told the court nothing pointed to a sexual assault or any sexual element, and, at a news conference after the sentencing, that there was no evidence of a background of violence or a criminal history before the murders, CNN reported.

The hearing on 23 July 2025 lasted about three hours, with more than a dozen impact statements. Funke's was read by a friend. She said she checked her room every night to be sure no one was hiding there. Mortensen, who said she was "barely 19" at the time, described panic attacks since the killings and having been forced to learn how to survive. Steve Goncalves turned the lectern to face Kohberger and said "Today, we're here to finish what you started." Kaylee's sister Alivea told him, "No one is scared of you today." Xana Kernodle's aunt told him she had forgiven him. Kohberger, in an orange jumpsuit, showed little reaction and "respectfully declined" to speak, Rolling Stone reported.

Hippler called him a "faceless coward" and said no conceivable reason could make sense of the crimes. "In my view, the time has now come to end Mr. Kohberger's 15 minutes of fame," he said, before sentencing him to prison "where he will remain until he dies". Beyond the life terms and the burglary sentence, NPR reported a $50,000 fine and a $5,000 civil penalty for each death. Kohberger is also required to provide a DNA sample under the deal. Hippler told him a notice of appeal could be filed within 40 days, but warned that filing one could breach the plea agreement.

The gag order on the lawyers ended with the sentencing, and court documents were released that evening. They included Funke's timeline of the last day and an account of Kohberger's first interview with police after his arrest. The records said he asked for a lawyer when officers began asking about the killings.

A year later Kohberger turned on his own plea. On the Sunday night before the filing he gave the New York Times a statement saying "My actual innocence is my truth" and that his plea had hinged on "false promises and blatant disinformation". On Monday 27 July 2026 he lodged a petition for post-conviction relief with the Ada County District Court, NBC News reported. The court record shows him representing himself. In it he says his lawyers gave him ineffective advice, that he was "convinced to falsely confess" to a crime he says he did not commit, and that he was told he would gain a "legal victory" from a "false plea".

Such a petition lets a convicted person challenge the conviction outside the ordinary appeals process, NBC explained. The plea agreement had waived his right to appeal. Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said his office "stands ready to do whatever is necessary to ensure justice is fully carried out". The Goncalves family called Kohberger "the mosquito you just can't seem to swat" and said the filing offered nothing beyond "a guilty man once again claiming he is innocent". His lawyers did not immediately reply to NBC's request for comment.

NBC noted that before the filing Kohberger had made no public statement suggesting he might change his plea. The central question, why the killings happened, was not answered by the plea and remains open.
